metadata.summary: This European consensus statement examines the history, indications, timing, operative techniques and complications of hemispheric disconnection for chronic drug-resistant epilepsy. It also describes practice across European epilepsy surgery centers and discusses approaches intended to reduce operative morbidity. Long-term seizure outcomes for minimally invasive disconnection remain uncertain because the available reports are limited.

care_settings: Dedicated postoperative medium or intensive care wards
target_population: Pediatric and adult patients with severe drug-resistant epilepsy arising predominantly from one diffusely affected hemisphere
Infants and young children considered for hemispheric disconnection

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe epilepsy whose seizures arise predominantly or entirely from one diffusely affected hemisphere, when a detailed evaluation suggests that the opposite hemisphere is healthy.
decision_rules: Severe drug resistance is an important prerequisite for hemispheric disconnection.

The survey reports that the choice between lateral and vertical functional disconnection strongly depends on the center where the epilepsy surgeon was trained; the cited comparisons do not establish one technique as generally preferable.
The procedure must disconnect the relevant unilateral efferent pathways and commissural connections to prevent seizure propagation to the opposite hemisphere.

recommended_regimens.name: Functional hemispherotomy
recommended_regimens.summary: Use functional hemispheric disconnection with limited tissue removal for appropriately selected unilateral epilepsy. The principal approaches are lateral and vertical, with several technical variants.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The document describes seizure freedom in a high percentage of patients and fewer complications than with extensive anatomical resection, without a reduction in the favorable seizure outcome percentage.

alternative_regimens.name: Vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Vertical functional disconnection is one of the principal operative approaches. Its steps include callosal, lateral, frontobasal, temporal and hippocampal disconnection.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: The approach and its variants depend on anatomy and the operating team's experience.

alternative_regimens.name: Periinsular hemispherotomy
alternative_regimens.summary: This lateral approach uses peri-insular access for hemispheric, callosal, temporal and insular disconnection.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: It is an operative variant rather than a universally preferred approach.

alternative_regimens.name: Transsylvian keyhole functional hemispherectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: This lateral keyhole variant provides access for frontobasal, callosal, temporal, hippocampal and insular disconnection through a smaller craniotomy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: It is especially suited to patients with some cerebral atrophy, including those with perinatal ischemic injury or Rasmussen encephalitis; hemimegalencephaly is a reason not to use the keyhole approach.

alternative_regimens.name: Japanese modified periinsular hemispherotomy
alternative_regimens.summary: This variant combines peri-insular and vertical operative elements, including callosal and temporomesial disconnection.

supportive_care: Transfer every patient to a dedicated medium- or intensive-care ward for at least one night.
Pediatric patients, particularly young infants, may require blood transfusion.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Hemispheric surgery requires an experienced interdisciplinary team, specialized operative and postoperative facilities, and extensive surgeon training with an experienced colleague. Only open disconnection procedures currently have reported long-term postoperative seizure outcomes; long-term seizure outcomes after minimally invasive approaches remain uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with drug-resistant epilepsy after perinatal infarction or intracerebral bleeding that has produced extensive unilateral hemispheric defects; many already have neurological deficits.
decision_rules: Consider hemispheric disconnection when seizures arise from the injured hemisphere and the opposite hemisphere is suitable for preserving function.
Neurological function may already have transferred partly to the healthy hemisphere, depending on whether the injury occurred intra-uterine or perinatally.

recommended_regimens.name: Hemispheric disconnection procedures (HDPs)
recommended_regimens.summary: Hemispheric disconnection is a classical surgical option for drug-resistant epilepsy caused by extensive perinatal hemispheric injury.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Schramm et al. reported postoperative seizure freedom rates of more than 90 % in the stroke-induced epilepsy group.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: An alternative disconnection procedure intended to avoid hemispherotomy has been described for stroke-induced epilepsy, but the document does not establish it as a preferred approach.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with predominantly unilateral HME and severe drug-resistant epilepsy, which commonly begins early after birth.
decision_rules: Consider surgical treatment early because drug resistance commonly develops early.
Account for the enlarged affected hemisphere, possible midline and superior sagittal sinus displacement, and distorted dysplastic anatomy when planning disconnection.
In general, use a larger craniotomy and remove more tissue, such as by standard temporal lobectomy, rather than relying on a transsylvian keyhole approach.

recommended_regimens.name: Hemispheric disconnection procedures (HDPs)
recommended_regimens.summary: Functional hemispheric disconnection is a treatment option for unilateral HME, with operative exposure and resection adapted to its enlarged and distorted anatomy.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Schramm et al. reported stable long-term seizure freedom in at least 60 % of cases; seizure control was less favorable than for the other conditions treated by HDP.

not_recommended.name: Transsylvian keyhole functional hemispherectomy
not_recommended.reason: The enlarged hemisphere and atypical insular cistern make HME an indication against the keyhole procedure.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A larger anatomical resection may sometimes permit clipping of MCA or ACA to reduce blood loss, but this could increase postoperative ischemia and brain edema. The document reports possible cognitive improvement in selected cases after hemispheric disconnection.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with drug-resistant epilepsy from cortical developmental malformations predominantly confined to one hemisphere, including multilobar focal cortical dysplasia or polymicrogyria.
decision_rules: Hemispheric disconnection can be considered when the malformation is predominantly unilateral.

recommended_regimens.name: Hemispheric disconnection procedures (HDPs)
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider disconnection for drug-resistant epilepsy associated with predominantly unilateral cortical developmental malformations.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with drug-resistant seizures and angiomatosis plaques strictly confined to one hemisphere.
decision_rules: Consider a disconnective procedure when drug resistance develops and the angiomatous involvement remains strictly unilateral.

Individualize surgical timing by weighing immediate neurological loss from disconnection against seizure burden and the risk of epileptogenic encephalopathy; incapacitating seizures may favor earlier surgery.

recommended_regimens.name: Hemispheric disconnection procedures (HDPs)
recommended_regimens.summary: Hemispheric disconnection is an option for drug-resistant seizures associated with strictly unilateral SWS involvement.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Kossoff et al. reported long-term seizure freedom in 80 % of patients.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The suspected epileptogenic zone may extend beyond visible angiomatosis plaques. The document identifies native bone-setting CT, contrast-enhanced T1W MRI and contrast-enhanced FLAIR as informative for defining the extent of pial angiomatosis.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with slow disease progression and mild or no neurological symptoms before a decision on hemispheric surgery.
decision_rules: Immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatment can be considered before surgery in patients with slowly progressive disease and limited neurological impairment.
Immune treatment should not be used as a reason to delay surgery, particularly if RE progresses rapidly.

alternative_regimens.name: immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatment
alternative_regimens.summary: Treatment before surgery may slow disease progression but does not cure RE; its effect on long-term outcome remains debated, and its effect on epilepsy is little or none.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider for slow progression with mild or absent neurological symptoms, without allowing it to postpone indicated surgery.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not specify an individual immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory regimen.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with RE causing drug-resistant unilateral seizures, including those with rapid progression or incapacitating seizures.
decision_rules: Functional hemispheric disconnection remains the only possible cure for seizures caused by RE.

Individualize timing by weighing seizure burden and the risk of epileptogenic encephalopathy against the immediate neurological impairment expected from disconnection, including hemiplegia and hemianopia.
Incapacitating seizures may favor earlier surgery to preserve the opportunity for neurological function to transfer to the healthy hemisphere.
For surgery on the language-dominant side, a thorough investigation with fMRI or Wada tests is advisable, depending on age, to estimate postoperative language risk.

recommended_regimens.name: Functional hemispheric disconnection
recommended_regimens.summary: Use functional hemispheric disconnection when pursuing seizure cure in RE, with timing determined by disease progression, seizure burden and anticipated neurological loss.

supportive_care: Rehabilitation is relevant after surgery; the document states that most patients regain independent walking, although fine finger movement remains impaired.
Intensive rehabilitation care may support long-term language recovery after dominant-side disconnection.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Dominant-side surgery presents an additional language risk. Publications cited by the document reported acute postoperative language worsening after left-sided functional HDP in pre- and young adolescent patients with RE, with possible longer-term recovery under intensive rehabilitation. The transsylvian keyhole approach is particularly suitable when RE has produced cerebral atrophy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Young infants with very severe unilateral epilepsy caused by acquired pathology or malformations of cortical development, particularly when neurological function is already impaired.
decision_rules: Determine surgical timing primarily from seizure severity and the underlying pathology.
Early surgery may prevent continued seizures from contributing to epileptogenic encephalopathy and adversely affecting the healthy hemisphere.
Very young age, low weight and low blood volume do not necessarily preclude surgery in an experienced epilepsy surgery center.

recommended_regimens.name: Hemispheric disconnection procedures (HDPs)
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider early hemispheric disconnection for severe unilateral epilepsy in appropriately selected infants at experienced centers.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a multicenter and multinational study including 48 hemispheric surgeries, surgery before the age of 3 months was not associated with more permanent morbidity or mortality than surgery in older infants.

supportive_care: Plan for the possibility of blood transfusion, especially in very young infants.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Experienced centers reported HDP from 4 months onward and described the possibility of operating at 2.5 months. The document identifies a high incidence of SUDEP among the severely affected infants discussed.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: A minority of patients with recurrent seizures after hemispheric surgery, or patients with HME and markedly distorted anatomy.
decision_rules: Classical anatomical hemispherectomy is still performed in a very small minority of cases at some epilepsy surgery centers, particularly for recurrent seizures or HME with substantially distorted anatomy.
Weigh its potential seizure effectiveness against the complications associated with extensive resection.

alternative_regimens.name: Anatomical hemispherectomy
alternative_regimens.summary: Complete anatomical hemispheric resection remains in use for a very small minority of selected cases at some epilepsy surgery centers.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider particularly for recurrent seizures or markedly distorted HME anatomy.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The procedure is time-consuming and associated with substantial complications. Older publications cited by the document reported mortality rates varying between 2 and 10 % for anatomical hemispherectomy.

toxicities.incidence: Earlier publications reported mortality of 2 to 10 % after anatomical hemispherectomy. Schramm et al. reported 1.0 % in a retrospective pediatric hemispherotomy series and 0 % in an adult series from the same center; several other recent pediatric series reported 0 %.
prevention: Limit tissue removal where feasible and avoid coagulating cortical vessels in the affected hemisphere; the document identifies these changes, together with advances in neuroanesthesia, as possible reasons for lower mortality.
During frontobasal disconnection, avoid injury to perforating arteries associated with the anterior communicating artery complex and ACA.

toxicities.incidence: Brian et al. reported transfusion in all cases in an older series. Gowda et al. reported transfusion in all cases in a series limited to children aged under 6 months. Roth et al. reported transfusion in all children undergoing hemispheric surgery before the age of 3 months.
recognition: Blood loss may be accompanied by tachycardia, circulatory instability, metabolic acidosis, hypothermia or severe electrolyte abnormalities.
Sagittal sinus injury can cause substantial bleeding.

management.actions: Provide a blood transfusion when needed; pediatric patients, particularly young infants, may require one.

prevention: Minimizing tissue resection and operative exposure has been associated with less blood loss and fewer transfusions.
For selected larger anatomical resections, clipping MCA or ACA may reduce blood loss, but could increase postoperative ischemia and brain edema.

toxicities.incidence: Lee et al. reported 9–81 % in mixed adult and pediatric populations and 23 % in pediatric series. Brotis et al. reported 2–26 %; more recently published pediatric series reported around 13–14 %, and Lopez et al. reported an overall incidence of 19 %.
recognition: The complication can arise early or late after anatomical hemispherectomy; delays of ten years or more have been described.
HME and multifocal cortical dysplasia have been proposed as conditions with greater postoperative risk.
prevention: Less extensive resection and more complete reliance on disconnection were adopted partly to reduce hydrocephalus.
Extensive intraoperative rinsing before closure might help prevent postoperative hydrocephalus.

Findings on EVD conflict: Lu et al. reported reduced postoperative hydrocephalus with routine drainage, whereas Sood et al. did not find an apparent reduction in definitive postoperative hydrocephalus. The document states that leaving a drain for a couple of days until CSF clears lacks a recommendation supported by clear evidence.
Giordano et al. developed an extraventricular variant specifically to reduce the possibility of postoperative hydrocephalus.

toxicities.incidence: For a composite of hematoma, infection and/or postoperative fever, Schramm et al. reported 7.4 % in adults and 9.7 % in children. Ye et al. reported 10 % for a composite of hematoma, hygroma and infection; Weil et al. reported 14.8 % for surgical complications. Lopez et al. found hematoma rates between 10 and 36 % across pediatric series.
recognition: Lopez et al. identified HME and SWS as conditions more frequently associated with postoperative hematoma.
prevention: The vertical midline technique describes meticulous hemostasis, saline irrigation of ventricular cavities and closure of ventricular access with fibrin glue to avoid a subdural collection.

toxicities.incidence: Lopez et al. observed persistent fever in up to 83 % of cases. Composite surgical morbidity rates that also include other events are reported under postoperative hematoma or hygroma.
recognition: A slight postoperative temperature rise occurs in almost all patients and is attributed to aseptic meningitis from blood products contaminating CSF.
Lopez et al. found postoperative fever more frequent with RE; Kamath et al. likewise reported a higher incidence with RE and less severe fevers with cortical dysplasia or polymicrogyria.
prevention: Routine EVD was reported by Lu et al. to reduce postoperative fever; Kamath et al. found that EVD use may lessen its occurrence.

toxicities.incidence: Lopez et al. reported postoperative infection rates from 2 % to 7 % in a review of 37 pediatric series. Other cited rates concern composites of infection with hematoma, hygroma and/or fever rather than infection alone.
recognition: Reported presentations include localized surgical wound infection and meningitis.
The historical complication was associated with neurological deterioration and could accompany hydrocephalus.
The document notes that its existence as a complication has been questioned and that recently published pediatric and adult series reported no cases.
prevention: Preserving and disconnecting tissue instead of undertaking extensive resection was intended to reduce this late complication.
The document proposes that reduced tissue destruction and blood loss may account for the absence of cases in recent series.

toxicities.event: SIADH, DI, cerebral salt wasting and severe electrolyte imbalance
recognition: Hypothalamic injury or ischemia during frontobasal disconnection can cause SIADH or DI; the document also identifies cerebral salt wasting as a possible cause of electrolyte imbalance.
Severe hypo- or hypernatremia may lead to sinus thrombosis, refractory brain edema, a life-threatening comatose state or death.
prevention: Avoid coagulating perforating arteries of the anterior communicating artery complex and ACA during frontobasal disconnection.

toxicities.event: Postoperative cerebral ischemia or brain edema
recognition: Sacrifice of multiple cortical veins during extensive resection can produce acute postoperative edema.
Clipping MCA or ACA in a larger anatomical resection could increase postoperative ischemia and edema.
Hypothalamic ischemia with severe electrolyte imbalance may result in refractory brain edema.
prevention: During anatomical hemispherectomy, preserve deep arterial perforators and avoid closing all large parasagittal bridging veins at the outset because the brain may swell.
Avoid coagulation of cortical vessels in the affected hemisphere and injury to perforators during frontobasal disconnection.

toxicities.incidence: Permanent worsening of preexisting hemiparesis or new hemiparesis was reported in the range of 8–21 %. Gowda et al. reported worsening in 8 % of pediatric cases; Ramantani et al. and Ghatan et al. each reported 10 %; Schusse et al. reported 21 % in an adult series.
recognition: Motor function on the side opposite surgery may decline, and fine finger movements can remain impaired.
The cited patients whose hemiparesis worsened remained ambulatory after surgery.

management.severity: Postoperative motor impairment in patients with RE
management.actions: The document reports that most patients regain independent walking after rehabilitation, although fine finger movement remains impaired.

toxicities.incidence: Schusse et al. observed postoperative worsening of language or speech in 10 % of adult cases.
recognition: Temporary mutism has been reported and resolved spontaneously.
Language symptoms occurred more frequently when the dominant hemisphere was involved.
In pre- and young adolescent patients with RE, left-sided functional HDP has been reported to worsen language acutely after surgery, with possible longer-term recovery under intensive rehabilitation.

management.severity: Acute postoperative language worsening in pre- and young adolescent patients with RE
management.actions: Intensive rehabilitation care may support longer-term recovery of language function, as described in cited publications.

prevention: For surgery on the language-dominant side in RE, the document advises a thorough preoperative investigation with fMRI or Wada tests, depending on age, to estimate the risk of postoperative language impairment.

toxicities.incidence: Chen et al. reported new or worsened strabismus in 49 % of pediatric cases. Meer et al. reported decreased visual acuity after surgery in 56 % of pediatric cases and new visual field deficits in 71 %.
recognition: A complete hemispheric disconnection inevitably produces postoperative hemianopia.
Visual acuity or visual fields may worsen, and new or worsened strabismus may occur.
Chen et al. reported compensatory torticollis in the vast majority of patients with new or worsened strabismus.

management.actions: The document states that compensatory mechanisms often limit functional impairment and that correction, including treatment of strabismus, may not be necessary.

recognition: The document states that postoperative neurocognitive effects have not been adequately investigated; the scarcity of reports does not establish an absence of effects.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Minimize brain tissue removal and avoid coagulating cortical vessels of the affected hemisphere where feasible to reduce procedure-related complications.
Avoid injuring the healthy contralateral hemisphere during disconnection.
Meticulous hemostasis followed by saline irrigation of ventricular cavities and closure of ventricular access with fibrin glue is described to avoid subdural collection.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients undergoing the described vertical midline approach

prophylaxis.recommendation: Extensive intraoperative rinsing before closure might help avoid postoperative hydrocephalus.

Although cited studies report reductions in postoperative fever or hydrocephalus with EVD, findings on definitive hydrocephalus conflict. Some centers leave a drain until CSF clears, but the document states that clear evidence does not support a recommendation for that practice.
prophylaxis.duration: A couple of days in centers that leave a drain until CSF clears

prophylaxis.recommendation: Transfer every patient to a dedicated medium- or intensive-care ward after surgery.

infection_management.prevention: The document attributes a common slight temperature rise to blood products in CSF and cites reports that EVD may reduce postoperative fever; it does not establish a clear recommendation for leaving a drain.

therapies_index.name: Hemispheric disconnection procedures (HDP)
therapies_index.mechanism: Disconnects the affected hemisphere to prevent seizures originating there from spreading.
approved_indications: Severe drug-resistant epilepsy arising predominantly or entirely from one extensively affected hemisphere when assessment suggests that the opposite hemisphere is healthy.
Unilateral acquired, congenital or progressive hemispheric pathology causing drug-resistant epilepsy.
therapies_index.administration: The procedures include lateral and vertical approaches, with variants that differ in the amount of tissue removed.
key_toxicities: Postoperative hydrocephalus, bleeding, hematoma, infection and fever.
Hemiparesis, hemianopia and possible language deterioration.
Hypothalamic injury during frontal disconnection can cause SIADH or DI and severe sodium disturbances.
monitoring: Transfer to a dedicated medium- or intensive-care ward for at least one night.

therapies_index.name: anatomical hemispherectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes an entire cerebral hemisphere while preserving the basal ganglia.
approved_indications: Historically used to treat epilepsy; still performed in a very small minority of cases, particularly for recurrent seizures or HME with markedly distorted anatomy.
therapies_index.administration: Requires extensive hemicraniotomy and hemispheric removal, which may be performed in more than one en bloc step.
key_toxicities: Earlier publications reported mortality rates varying between 2 and 10 %.
Major intraoperative blood loss and postoperative cerebral edema.
Hydrocephalus, superficial cerebral hemosiderosis, hematoma, persistent fever and infection.
monitoring: Transfer to a dedicated medium- or intensive-care ward for at least one night.

therapies_index.name: hemidecortication
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes the epileptogenic cerebral cortex rather than the whole hemisphere.
approved_indications: Described as a less extensive anatomical operation for epilepsy.

therapies_index.name: functional hemispherectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Disconnects hemispheric pathways while removing less cerebral tissue than anatomical hemispherectomy.
approved_indications: Drug-resistant epilepsy arising from a diffusely affected hemisphere.
The European center survey also reports its use for hemimegalencephaly.
therapies_index.administration: Functional techniques disconnect unilateral projection and commissural pathways, including the corpus callosum, while limiting resection.
key_toxicities: Postoperative hydrocephalus, blood loss, hematoma, infection and fever.
Neurological deterioration, including motor, visual or language impairment.
SIADH or DI may follow hypothalamic injury during frontal disconnection.
monitoring: Transfer to a dedicated medium- or intensive-care ward for at least one night.

therapies_index.name: functional hemispherotomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Functionally isolates the diseased hemisphere with relatively little tissue removal.
approved_indications: Severe unilateral drug-resistant epilepsy associated with acquired lesions, malformations of cortical development or progressive pathology.
therapies_index.administration: Can be performed through lateral or vertical approaches; complete disconnection includes unilateral projection and commissural pathways.
key_toxicities: Postoperative hydrocephalus, hemorrhage, hematoma, infection and fever.
Possible worsening of motor, visual or language function; complete hemispheric disconnection inevitably causes postoperative hemianopia.
Potentially life-threatening sodium disturbances after hypothalamic injury.
monitoring: Transfer to a dedicated medium- or intensive-care ward for at least one night.

therapies_index.name: Rasmussen’s functional hemispherectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines limited cortical and temporal resection with callosotomy and disconnection of the remaining frontal, parietal and occipital regions.
approved_indications: Epilepsy treated by hemispheric surgery.
therapies_index.administration: Resects a frontoparietal region and performs temporal lobectomy, callosotomy and disconnection of the remaining involved lobes.

therapies_index.name: Vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Disconnects callosal, lateral hemispheric, frontobasal and temporomesial pathways through a predominantly parasagittal route.
approved_indications: Unilateral drug-resistant epilepsy requiring hemispheric disconnection.
therapies_index.administration: Uses a frontal opening to reach the lateral ventricle, followed by callosal, posterior fornix, lateral, temporal and frontobasal disconnections. Neuronavigation is advisable, particularly when anatomy is distorted.
key_toxicities: Postoperative hydrocephalus and other complications of hemispheric disconnection.
monitoring: Transfer to a dedicated medium- or intensive-care ward for at least one night.

therapies_index.name: vertical midline approach
therapies_index.mechanism: Achieves hemispheric disconnection through an interhemispheric callosotomy followed by lateral, anterior and temporal disconnections.
approved_indications: Unilateral drug-resistant epilepsy requiring hemispheric disconnection.
therapies_index.administration: An interhemispheric route exposes the corpus callosum; after callosotomy, the ventricle is opened for lateral, anterior and temporal disconnection. The ventricular opening is closed with fibrin glue after saline irrigation and hemostasis.
key_toxicities: CSF leakage, brain collapse and subdural collection are concerns addressed by the described operative steps.

therapies_index.name: Periinsular hemispherotomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Disconnects the hemisphere through openings above and below the insula, with callosal, frontal, temporal and insular disconnection.
approved_indications: Unilateral drug-resistant epilepsy requiring hemispheric disconnection.
therapies_index.administration: A craniotomy over the Sylvian fissure provides suprainsular and infrainsular access. The operation includes callosotomy, frontal and temporal disconnections, temporomesial resection and insular disconnection.
key_toxicities: Postoperative complications of hemispheric disconnection; comparative studies cited in the consensus give differing results on the safety of specific approaches.

therapies_index.name: Transsylvian keyhole functional hemispherectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Disconnects the affected hemisphere through a small transsylvian opening, including temporomesial, frontobasal, callosal and insular steps.
approved_indications: Unilateral drug-resistant epilepsy, particularly when brain atrophy is present, such as after perinatal ischemic events or in RE.
therapies_index.administration: A small craniotomy centered on the Sylvian fissure permits temporal horn entry, unco-amygala-hippocampectomy, frontobasal disconnection, intraventricular callosotomy and insular aspiration. HME is described as a reason not to use the keyhole procedure because of hemispheric enlargement and atypical anatomy.
key_toxicities: Potential injury to the healthy contralateral hemisphere, which the operation must strictly avoid.

therapies_index.name: Japanese modified periinsular hemispherotomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Combines peri-insular and vertical disconnection elements to interrupt callosal and temporomesial connections.
approved_indications: Epilepsy requiring hemispheric disconnection.
therapies_index.administration: Uses a craniotomy spanning the lateral ventricle, frontal opercular resection and upper insular corticectomy, followed by callosotomy and amygdalo-hippocampectomy.

therapies_index.name: Modified vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy
approved_indications: Reported among the hemispheric disconnection techniques used by surveyed European centers for unilateral drug-resistant epilepsy.

therapies_index.name: vertical extraventricular functional hemispherotomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides an extraventricular route for hemispheric disconnection.
approved_indications: Described as a hemispheric disconnection variant intended particularly to reduce postoperative hydrocephalus.

therapies_index.name: Endoscope-assisted hemispherotomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Performs functional hemispheric disconnection with endoscopic assistance through a smaller opening.
approved_indications: Reported in pediatric patients with chronic epilepsy caused by perinatal strokes.
therapies_index.administration: Follows an approach resembling vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy, with interhemispheric callosotomy and anterior, middle, posterior and hippocampal disconnections through a smaller incision and craniotomy.
key_toxicities: A longer operation could possibly increase complications such as infection compared with open surgery, but the limited literature does not clearly establish this.

therapies_index.name: MRgLITT
therapies_index.mechanism: Applies laser energy through stereotactically placed probes to ablate predefined brain tissue under real-time MRI guidance.
approved_indications: Reported for hemispheric disconnection in a pediatric patient whose multiple comorbidities made open disconnection unsuitable; the consensus states that this first case does not permit a definitive recommendation.
The literature discussed also reports LITT treatment of epileptogenic lesions and corpus callosotomy.
therapies_index.administration: The reported hemispheric disconnection used 5 laser catheters placed across the hemisphere.

therapies_index.name: radiofrequency (RF) ablation
therapies_index.mechanism: Uses radiofrequency thermocoagulation for targeted tissue disconnection.
approved_indications: Reported as a robotic technique for hemispheric disconnection using the same technical concept as MRIgLITT; long-term seizure outcomes remain uncertain.
therapies_index.administration: Robotic thermocoagulation is described, without a detailed procedural schedule.

therapies_index.name: posterior disconnection
therapies_index.mechanism: Disconnects a more circumscribed posterior region rather than the entire hemisphere.
approved_indications: Mentioned as a more localized epilepsy operation; the center survey reports a posterior disconnection for tuberous sclerosis.

therapies_index.name: corpus callosotomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Interrupts callosal fibers to prevent seizure spread between hemispheres.
approved_indications: Described as part of functional hemispheric disconnection; open and laser-based callosotomy are also discussed.
therapies_index.administration: Can be performed through open surgical approaches or, in the literature reviewed, by laser ablation.

therapies_index.name: temporal lobectomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Removes temporal lobe tissue as part of hemispheric surgery.
approved_indications: Described as part of Rasmussen’s functional hemispherectomy and as an option when HME anatomy makes a keyhole procedure unsuitable.
therapies_index.administration: The consensus suggests a standard temporal lobectomy as an example of the larger resection generally recommended for HME.

therapies_index.name: frontoparietal operculum resection
approved_indications: Presented as an alternative to a keyhole procedure when HME causes hemispheric enlargement and atypical anatomy.

therapies_index.name: Motor sparing functional hemispherectomy
approved_indications: Listed among the hemispheric operations reported in the European center survey.

therapies_index.name: immunosuppressive treatment
approved_indications: Can be considered before surgery for RE, particularly with slow progression and mild or absent neurological symptoms. The consensus states that it may slow the disease but does not cure RE, has little or no effect on epilepsy, and should not delay surgery, especially when RE progresses rapidly.

therapies_index.name: immunomodulatory treatment
approved_indications: Can be considered before surgery for RE, particularly with slow progression and mild or absent neurological symptoms. The consensus states that it may slow the disease but does not cure RE, has little or no effect on epilepsy, and should not delay surgery, especially when RE progresses rapidly.

therapies_index.name: anti-seizure medication (ASM)
approved_indications: Mentioned in the context of epilepsy treatment and its potential effect on comparisons between surgical series; severe drug resistance is an important prerequisite for hemispheric disconnection.

therapies_index.name: routine external ventricular drainage (EVD)
approved_indications: Discussed for management after hemispheric surgery. One cited study reported less postoperative fever and hydrocephalus, while findings on prevention of definitive postoperative hydrocephalus differ between centers; the consensus states that leaving a drain in place for several days lacks a recommendation supported by clear evidence.
therapies_index.administration: In some centers, the drain remains in place for a couple of days until the CSF clears.
monitoring: CSF clearing is used by some centers to determine when to remove the drain.

therapies_index.name: shunt insertion
approved_indications: Postoperative hydrocephalus requiring a shunt after hemispheric surgery.

therapies_index.name: blood transfusion
approved_indications: May be needed after hemispheric surgery in pediatric patients, particularly young infants, or during surgery when blood loss is substantial.

therapies_index.name: rehabilitation
approved_indications: Described after hemispheric disconnection for RE; most patients regain independent walking, although fine finger movements remain impaired. Intensive rehabilitation is also described in reports of long-term language recovery after dominant-side disconnection in young patients.

conditions.name: drug-resistant epilepsy
conditions.description: Severe epilepsy arising predominantly or entirely from a diffusely affected hemisphere is the principal indication for hemispheric disconnection when assessment suggests that the opposite hemisphere is healthy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Candidates frequently already have hemiparesis, hemianopia and some degree of neuropsychological impairment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish that seizures arise predominantly or entirely from one diffusely damaged hemisphere and assess the contralateral hemisphere.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A contralateral hemisphere judged healthy supports consideration of the procedure.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess language lateralization for preoperative counseling.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Children older than 5–7 years with disease affecting the dominant hemisphere.

long_term_effects: Complete hemispheric disconnection inevitably produces postoperative hemianopia, although it usually does not limit function.
Changes in contralateral motor function and language are difficult to predict before surgery.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The document states that the neurocognitive effects of hemispherotomy have not been sufficiently studied.

conditions.name: Perinatal middle cerebral artery (MCA) infarction
conditions.description: A perinatal infarct can leave extensive hemispheric defects with multiple cysts and cause drug-resistant epilepsy. In patients with stroke-induced epilepsy, an alternative disconnection procedure that avoids hemispherotomy has also been described.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Most affected candidates have a neurological deficit. Depending on whether the injury occurred in utero or perinatally, neurological functions may have transferred partly to the unaffected hemisphere. An illustrated case involved a 4yrs old child with delayed motor development, refractory seizures for 18 months and left hemiparesis who could walk.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Depict the hemispheric infarct and its anatomical involvement.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The illustrated perinatal MCA-infarction involved the pyramidal tract.

long_term_effects: A cited series reported postoperative seizure freedom of more than 90 % in this group.

conditions.name: intracerebral bleeding
conditions.description: Perinatal intracerebral bleeding can result in extensive hemispheric defects containing numerous cysts. When it causes drug-resistant epilepsy, the document identifies it as a classical indication for hemispheric disconnection.

conditions.name: hemimegalencephaly
conditions.description: A congenital dysplastic developmental malformation involving abnormal enlargement of one hemisphere or some of its lobes, often arising from disturbed neuronal migration. Disease predominantly confined to one hemisphere can be considered for hemispheric disconnection. The enlarged and dysplastic hemisphere may distort the midline, displace the superior sagittal sinus and obscure the distinction between gray and white matter.
conditions.epidemiology: Seizures occur in more than 90 % of affected patients and usually begin early after birth.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Severe drug-resistant epilepsy typically accompanies a contralateral motor deficit and cognitive impairment. Drug resistance tends to develop early.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess enlargement, displacement of midline structures and complex dysplastic anatomy when planning disconnection.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The affected hemisphere may be enlarged, with midline shift or displacement of the superior sagittal sinus.

long_term_effects: A cited series reported sustained long-term seizure freedom in at least 60 % of cases after hemispheric disconnection.
A cited publication described cognitive improvement in selected cases.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The document reports less seizure control after disconnection for HME than for the other conditions treated by hemispheric disconnection.

conditions.name: focal cortical dysplasia
conditions.description: The document includes focal cortical dysplasia among the multi-lobar cortical malformations. Hemispheric disconnection can be considered when a malformation of cortical development is predominantly limited to one hemisphere and causes drug-resistant epilepsy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Drug-resistant epilepsy is the clinical feature identified for this group of malformations.

conditions.name: polymicrogyria
conditions.description: The document identifies polymicrogyria as a multi-lobar cortical malformation. Hemispheric disconnection can be considered for a malformation of cortical development predominantly restricted to one hemisphere when it causes drug-resistant epilepsy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Drug-resistant epilepsy is the clinical feature identified for this group of malformations.

conditions.name: Sturge-Weber syndrome
conditions.description: A rare, sporadic neurocutaneous disorder in which extensive pial angiomatosis can cause seizures. Angiomatosis may be confined to one lobe or extend across a hemisphere. The document notes a presumption that the epileptogenic cortex can extend beyond the angiomatous plaques. Strict confinement of the plaques to one hemisphere makes patients who develop drug resistance candidates for disconnection.
conditions.epidemiology: Seizures occur in 75 %–90 % of cases, and approximately 60 % of patients develop drug resistance.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Types 1 and 2 can be suspected from a characteristic facial port-wine stain angioma; type 3 has leptomeningeal angiomatosis without that readily recognizable presentation.

subtypes.name: type 1
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A characteristic facial port-wine stain angioma makes this variant easier to suspect.

subtypes.name: type 2
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A characteristic facial port-wine stain angioma makes this variant easier to suspect.

subtypes.name: type 3
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Only leptomeningeal angiomatosis is described, making recognition less straightforward.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help delineate the extent of pial angiomatosis, including calcified areas.
Help define the distribution of pial angiomatosis.
Delineate the extent of pial angiomatosis.

long_term_effects: A cited study reported long-term seizure freedom in 80 % of patients.

conditions.name: Rasmussen encephalitis
conditions.description: A rare disorder involving inflammation that usually remains confined to one hemisphere despite its immunological background. It produces progressive hemispheric atrophy, neurological deterioration, cognitive decline and drug-resistant epilepsy. Recent findings cited by the document suggest a T-cell-driven inflammatory response.
conditions.epidemiology: The estimated incidence is 2.4 cases in 1,000,000. Drug resistance develops in almost all cases, and about 50 % of affected patients develop epilepsia partialis continua (EPC).
conditions.clinical_presentation: Epilepsy and worsening neurological function usually signal the start of the acute stage. Progression can culminate in hemiplegia and, when the dominant hemisphere is involved, aphasia. An illustrated case involved a 13yrs old child with left-arm epilepsia partialis continua and progressive hemiparesis. Initial hemiparesis may nevertheless be mild, complicating the timing of surgery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify progressive atrophy of the affected hemisphere.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Atrophy is unilateral and usually begins in the insular lobe.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Depict hemispheric metabolic abnormalities in the illustrated case.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The illustrated case showed right-hemisphere hypometabolism.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate the risk of postoperative language impairment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider for surgery affecting the language-dominant hemisphere, according to patient age.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Estimate the risk of postoperative language impairment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Consider for surgery affecting the language-dominant hemisphere, according to patient age.

definitions.description: The stage preceding the acute phase; the document provides no further defining features.
Lasts 8–12 months and typically begins with epilepsy and neurological deterioration, accompanied by progressive unilateral hemispheric atrophy.
The stage following the acute phase; the document provides no further defining features.

long_term_effects: After hemispheric disconnection, most patients regain independent walking with rehabilitation, although fine finger movements remain impaired.

Cited publications report that language may worsen soon after left-sided dominant-hemisphere disconnection in pre- and young adolescent patients, then recover over the long term with intensive rehabilitation.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The document describes functional hemispheric disconnection as the only cure for seizures caused by RE. It states that immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatment can slow the disease but has little or no effect on epilepsy; whether it improves long-term outcome remains debated.

conditions.name: HHE syndrome
conditions.description: Listed among the hemispheric conditions treated with disconnection at surveyed centers.

conditions.name: Tuberous sclerosis
conditions.description: Listed among conditions treated at surveyed centers; one center associates it with posterior disconnection. Another reports patients with tuberous sclerosis complex when HME or another hemispheric abnormality was also present.

special_populations.considerations: Infants with severe seizures caused by acquired pathology or malformations of cortical development may already have neurological impairment and face a high risk of sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP). Low weight and blood volume complicate surgery. Experienced centers report performing hemispheric disconnection from 4 months onward, with a possible lower limit of 2.5 months. In a study of surgery before the age of 3 months that included 48 hemispheric surgeries, Roth et al. found no greater permanent morbidity or mortality than in older infants; all children undergoing hemispheric surgery before the age of 3 months received blood transfusions.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Surgery in very young infants can be undertaken at experienced epilepsy surgery centers; a blood transfusion may be needed.

special_populations.population: Children older than 5–7 years with dominant-hemisphere pathology
special_populations.considerations: The timing of disconnection is particularly difficult when the affected hemisphere is language-dominant. Resting state-fMRI can identify language lateralization in children and may assist preoperative counseling.

special_populations.population: Patients with Rasmussen encephalitis and mild neurological impairment
special_populations.considerations: Surgical timing is difficult when drug-resistant seizures develop before substantial hemiparesis. Immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatment may slow disease progression, particularly when progression is slow and neurological symptoms are mild or absent, but it has little to no effect on epilepsy and cannot cure Rasmussen encephalitis.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatment can be considered before surgery in patients with slow progression and mild or absent neurological symptoms. It should not delay surgery, especially when disease progression is rapid.

special_populations.population: Patients with Rasmussen encephalitis affecting the language-dominant hemisphere
special_populations.considerations: The potential loss of language function makes surgical timing especially difficult. Published reports describe acute postoperative language worsening after left-sided functional hemispheric disconnection in pre- and young adolescent patients, with possible longer-term recovery under intensive rehabilitation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Depending on age, thorough preoperative assessment with fMRI or Wada tests is advisable to estimate the risk of postoperative language impairment.

special_populations.population: Patients with hemimegalencephaly and enlarged or distorted hemispheric anatomy
special_populations.considerations: The affected hemisphere may be enlarged, with midline displacement, a shifted superior sagittal sinus and poorly defined gray-white matter boundaries. An atypical insular cistern can make the transsylvian keyhole procedure unsuitable.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: A larger craniotomy and more extensive tissue resection are generally recommended; a standard temporal lobectomy is one example. Temporal lobectomy or frontoparietal operculum resection is proposed instead of the keyhole procedure when anatomy makes that approach unsuitable.

special_populations.population: Patients with multiple comorbidities unsuitable for open disconnective surgery
special_populations.considerations: A pediatric case with multiple comorbidities was treated using laser-based hemispheric disconnection because open surgery was unsuitable. As this was the first reported case, the document offers no definitive conclusion or advice about this approach.

recommendations.statement: Hemispheric disconnection procedures (HDPs) may be considered when malformations of cortical development predominantly affect one hemisphere.
recommendations.context: The conditions discussed include hemimegalencephaly (HME) and multi-lobar cortical malformations associated with drug-resistant epilepsy.
recommendations.rationale: Both groups can cause drug-resistant epilepsy.

recommendations.statement: Consider surgical treatment early in patients with HME.
recommendations.rationale: Seizures usually begin early after birth, and drug resistance typically develops early.

recommendations.statement: Immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatment may be considered before surgery, particularly for patients with slowly progressive RE and mild or absent neurological symptoms.
recommendations.rationale: Such treatment can slow disease progression, although its effect on epilepsy is limited or absent.

recommendations.statement: Do not postpone surgery because immune treatment is being given, especially when RE progresses rapidly.
recommendations.rationale: Immune treatments do not cure RE and have little to no effect on its epilepsy.

recommendations.statement: Weigh the potential for seizure cure with a functional hemispheric disconnection procedure against the resulting neurological impairment, including hemiplegia and hemianopia.
recommendations.rationale: Functional hemispheric disconnection is presented as the only possible cure for seizures caused by RE.

recommendations.statement: For surgery on the language-dominant side, a thorough preoperative investigation with fMRI or Wada tests is advisable, depending on the patient's age, to estimate the risk of postoperative language impairment.
recommendations.context: Planning the timing and decision for surgery in RE.
recommendations.rationale: Predicting language consequences is especially challenging when the affected hemisphere is language-dominant.

recommendations.statement: Hemispheric disconnection surgery can be performed in very young children at experienced epilepsy surgery centers despite their low weight and blood volume.
recommendations.context: Timing of surgery in young infants with severe epilepsy.
recommendations.rationale: The document cites experience with surgery in very young infants and emphasizes the potential benefit of earlier seizure cessation.

recommendations.statement: Determine the timing of disconnection individually in progressive conditions such as SWS and RE, weighing the immediate loss of neurological function against seizure burden and the risk of epileptogenic encephalopathy.
recommendations.context: Earlier surgery may be favored when seizures are incapacitating.
recommendations.rationale: Earlier seizure control may preserve an opportunity for neurological function to transfer to the healthy hemisphere.

recommendations.statement: During anatomical hemispherectomy, avoid closing all large parasagittal bridging veins at the outset.
recommendations.context: Division and clipping of cerebral vessels during the procedure.
recommendations.rationale: Early closure of these veins risks brain swelling.

recommendations.statement: Neuronavigation is advisable for vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy, particularly when anatomy is distorted, to guide placement of the craniotomy.
recommendations.context: Planning sufficient access for anterior disconnection.

recommendations.statement: Strictly avoid injuring the healthy contralateral hemisphere during transsylvian keyhole functional hemispherectomy.
In patients with HME, generally use a larger craniotomy and remove a greater volume of tissue, for example by performing a standard temporal lobectomy.
recommendations.context: Adaptation of hemispheric disconnection techniques to HME.
recommendations.rationale: The affected hemisphere may be enlarged, displaced and anatomically complex because of dysplastic tissue.

recommendations.statement: Transfer every patient to a dedicated medium-care or intensive-care ward for at least one night after surgery.
Before performing hemispheric surgery, the epilepsy surgeon should undertake extensive training with a colleague experienced in these procedures.
recommendations.rationale: Hemispheric surgery is highly complex and requires an experienced interdisciplinary team and specialized operative and postoperative facilities.
