document_sections.heading: A B S T R A C T
document_sections.content: Introduction: Surgery for severe drug-resistant epilepsy arising from one hemisphere is technically demanding. Over recent decades, anatomical hemispherectomy has largely given way to functional hemispherotomy, with fewer complications and similarly favorable seizure outcomes. An EANS Section for Functional Neurosurgery task force developed a European consensus on hemispheric disconnection. Research question and methods: The authors examined the history, indications, timing, techniques, complications and European practice of these procedures for drug-resistant epilepsy. They searched relevant literature using PRISMA 2020 guidance. Results: The statement reviews the evolution of surgery, clinical selection, operative timing and methods, complications, and practices at European epilepsy centers. Knowledge of long-term seizure outcomes comes mainly from open procedures; reports of minimally invasive approaches are limited to individual cases or small series, so their long-term outcomes remain uncertain. Discussion and conclusion: The authors describe this as the first European consensus addressing these aspects of disconnection for chronic drug-resistant epilepsy and as a comprehensive account of practice at participating European centers.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: Perinatal stroke, Rasmussen encephalitis, hemimegalencephaly and Sturge-Weber syndrome can produce severe drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE), particularly in children, with increased morbidity and mortality. Hemispheric disconnection procedures (HDP) are established potentially curative operations that achieve seizure freedom in a high proportion of patients. During the 20th century, surgery progressed from extensive anatomical removal to functional disconnection with little tissue resection; this reduced perioperative complications without reducing favorable seizure outcomes. Vertical and lateral disconnection are the principal functional approaches, each with variants. More recent options include magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided laser interstitial thermal therapy and radiofrequency ablation. Because long-term follow-up for these minimally invasive approaches is unavailable, definitive seizure outcomes cannot yet be compared with open operations. Members of the European Association of Neurosurgical Societies (EANS) functional neurosurgery section and invited European epilepsy surgeons present a consensus on the history, indications, timing, techniques, complications and current European use of HDP.

document_sections.heading: 2. Methods
document_sections.content: The authors sought literature relevant to HDP for drug-resistant epilepsy in PubMed, Embase and the Cochrane Library. They applied the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidance and its extension for Scoping Reviews where appropriate. Exploratory searching informed combinations of hemispherectomy, hemispheric surgery, hemispherotomy, hemidecortication, hemicorticectomy, (drug-resistant or intractable) epilepsy, and seizure with terms for history, indication, timing, surgical technique, complications and practice. The last search occurred on February 25, 2023; publication dates were unrestricted, and reference lists supplied additional publications. The search identified 626 articles. Titles and abstracts were screened for relevance to history, indications, timing, techniques, complications or current practice. Eligible publications were peer-reviewed research or reviews, including retrospective and prospective studies of pediatric or adult HDP for drug-resistant epilepsy. Non-epileptic indications, procedures without disconnection, articles in non-European languages, editorials, notes, letters and single-case reports were excluded. Full texts were obtained for applicable articles. The PICO question defined pediatric and adult patients with drug-resistant epilepsy as the population; any HDP as intervention and comparison; and indications, timing, anatomical or functional techniques, newer developments and complications, including avoidance, as outcomes. An EANS task force and invited European specialists interpreted the literature, discussed the topics and reached consensus. Co-authors also completed a questionnaire about practice at their centers; Table 1 presents their answers.

document_sections.heading: 3. History
document_sections.content: Goltz and Van Mering reported experiments on mammals after hemispheric resections at the end of the 19th century. Goltz described post-resection behavior; one studied dog survived 18 months and showed marked atrophy and scarring at dissection. In 1928, Dandy reported five patients who underwent hemispheric removal for malignant gliomas: all developed left-sided paralysis, three had altered consciousness, two died after 2 days and two weeks respectively, and one survived 3.5 years. Krynauw published the first epilepsy-focused hemispheric surgery series in 1950: among 12 patients, all had a preoperative hemi-syndrome, 10 had convulsions of differing kinds, and the oldest was 21 years old. Most underwent surface EEG and ventriculography. Krynauw considered language transfer after early injury and ipsilateral motor representation, and described substantial improvements in behavior, personality and mental functioning. In a 1982 lecture, Rasmussen reviewed the Montreal experience and linked anatomical hemispherectomy to frequent early and late hydrocephalus, sometimes appearing ten years or more after surgery. His team reduced resection while disconnecting and retaining larger portions of the hemisphere; seizure results remained promising. Rasmussen considered subtotal anatomical removal with complete functional disconnection capable of maintaining therapeutic effect while protecting against late superficial cerebral hemosiderosis, neurological deterioration, hydrocephalus and sometimes death. This development helped motivate lateral transsylvian and vertical hemispherotomy. More broadly, surgeons moved from large excisions toward predominantly disconnective operations to limit exposure and complications, provided seizure control was preserved; the principle also extends to more limited operations such as posterior disconnection.

document_sections.heading: 4. Indications
document_sections.content: HDP is generally used for severe or catastrophic drug-resistant epilepsy when most or all seizures arise from one diffusely damaged hemisphere and detailed evaluation suggests that the opposite hemisphere is healthy. Many candidates already have hemiparesis, hemianopia or neuropsychological impairment. Severe drug resistance is an important prerequisite. The underlying conditions are grouped as acquired, congenital or progressive.

document_sections.heading: 4.1. Acquired pathologies
document_sections.content: Acquired hemispheric injury is one category of conditions considered for HDP.

document_sections.heading: 4.1.1. Perinatal middle cerebral artery (MCA) infarction
document_sections.content: Perinatal infarction or intracerebral hemorrhage can leave extensive hemispheric defects and multiple cysts associated with drug-resistant epilepsy; this is a classical indication for hemispheric disconnection. An alternative disconnection avoiding hemispherotomy has been described particularly for stroke-related epilepsy. Most affected patients have a neurological deficit. Depending on whether the injury occurred intra-uterine or perinatally, some neurological functions may already have shifted to the unaffected hemisphere, making these patients particularly suitable candidates. Reported postoperative seizure freedom in this group exceeds 90 %. Fig. 1 depicts a 4yrs old male with delayed motor development, refractory seizures for 18 months and left hemiparesis who could walk; transversal and coronar T2 weighted MRI show a perinatal MCA-infarction involving the pyramidal tract.

document_sections.heading: 4.2. Congenital pathologies
document_sections.content: Congenital indications include malformations of cortical development.

document_sections.heading: 4.2.1. Malformations of cortical development (MCD)
document_sections.content: The two main groups are hemimegalencephaly (HME) and multilobar malformations, including focal cortical dysplasia and polymicrogyria. Although distinct, both commonly present with drug resistant epilepsy (DRE). HDP can be considered when a malformation is predominantly confined to one hemisphere. HME is a congenital dysplastic developmental abnormality with excessive growth of a hemisphere or some of its lobes, often linked to disordered neuronal migration. Typical features are severe DRE, contralateral motor impairment and cognitive impairment. Seizures usually start early after birth and affect more than 90 % of patients; drug resistance generally develops early, supporting early consideration of surgery. Compared with other HDP indications, seizure control after HME disconnection is less favorable, but long-term seizure freedom is achievable in at least 60 % of cases, and selected patients can improve cognitively.

document_sections.heading: Table 1 Overview of European hospitals performing hemispheric disconnective procedures for epilepsy.
document_sections.content: The table reports participating centers by country and describes when HDP began, numbers of centers and surgeons, annual procedure volume, operative approaches and variants, center-reported differences in complications, indications, patient age groups and recent changes in procedure frequency. Its responses represent center reports rather than comparative evidence establishing superiority of an approach.

document_sections.heading: 4.3. Progressive pathologies
document_sections.content: Progressive hemispheric conditions discussed as HDP indications include Sturge-Weber syndrome and Rasmussen encephalitis. Their evolving neurological deficits make operative timing particularly difficult.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.1. Sturge-Weber-syndrome
document_sections.content: Sturge-Weber syndrome (SWS) is an uncommon sporadic neurocutaneous disorder, formerly categorized as a phakomatosis. Among its three variants, types 1 and 2 are suggested by a characteristic facial port-wine angioma, whereas type 3 has leptomeningeal angiomatosis without that readily visible feature. Seizures occur in 75 %–90 % of cases. Extensive pial angiomatosis causes seizures and can affect one lobe or much of a hemisphere; the epileptogenic cortex is presumed to extend beyond visible angiomatous plaques. Native bone-setting computed tomography (CT), contrast-enhanced T1W MRI and especially contrast-enhanced fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) help define the extent of calcified pial angiomatosis. Approximately 60 % of patients develop drug resistance. Patients whose plaques remain strictly unilateral are suitable candidates for disconnection, with reported long-term seizure freedom of 80 %.

document_sections.heading: 4.3.2. Rasmussen encephalitis
document_sections.content: Rasmussen encephalitis (RE) is a rare unilateral inflammatory neurological disease, with an estimated incidence of 2.4 cases in 1,000,000. It involves progressive neurological and cognitive decline alongside drug-resistant epilepsy. Recent findings suggest T-cell-driven inflammation. Its typical course comprises a prodromal stage, an acute stage lasting 8–12 months and a residual stage. Neurological deterioration and epilepsy generally signal the acute stage; MRI can identify progressively worsening unilateral atrophy, usually beginning in the insula. Despite the disease's immunological background, it usually affects only one hemisphere. Hemiplegia and, with dominant-hemisphere disease, aphasia may develop. Drug resistance occurs in almost all cases, and about 50 % develop epilepsia partialis continua (EPC). HDP is the only curative seizure treatment. Surgery can be difficult to time because early hemiparesis is often mild. Immunosuppressive or immunomodulatory treatment can slow progression and may be suitable before surgery, especially with slow progression and mild or absent neurological symptoms; whether it improves long-term outcome remains debated, and it does not cure RE. Its effect on epilepsy is little or absent, so it should not delay surgery, particularly during rapid progression. The prospect of seizure cure must be balanced against hemiplegia and hemianopia. Most patients regain independent walking with rehabilitation, although fine finger movements remain impaired. For operations on the language-dominant side, age-dependent preoperative fMRI or Wada assessment is advisable to estimate language risk. Publications on pre- and young adolescent patients report acute language deterioration after left dominant-side functional HDP, followed by possible longer-term recovery with intensive rehabilitation. Fig. 2 shows a 13yrs old male with left-arm EPC and progressive hemiparesis; FDG-PET/CT and T2 weighted MRI demonstrate right-hemisphere hypometabolism and slight hemiatrophy.

document_sections.heading: 5. Timing
document_sections.content: Seizure severity and underlying disease chiefly determine when HDP is performed. Decision-making can be relatively direct for young infants with very severe epilepsy from acquired injury or cortical malformation, existing neurological impairment and high sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) risk. Experienced centers can operate despite low infant weight and blood volume: published experience includes surgery from 4 months onward, a possible lower limit of 2.5 months, and ultra-early surgery before 3 months. A multinational multicenter study involving 48 hemispheric surgeries found no greater permanent morbidity or mortality with surgery before 3 months than with operations in older infants. Earlier seizure cessation may improve long-term outcomes and prevent epileptogenic encephalopathy that could adversely affect the healthy hemisphere. In progressive SWS and especially RE, the immediate neurological loss from disconnection must be balanced individually against seizure burden and the risk of epileptogenic encephalopathy. Incapacitating seizures can favor earlier surgery while neurological function might still transfer to the unaffected side. Surgery on a dominant hemisphere is also difficult to time in children older than 5–7 years. Resting state-fMRI can establish language lateralization in children and aid counseling. Clinical experience described in the cited literature suggests cognitive safety across ages regardless of language dominance, with postoperative status often resembling preoperative status.

document_sections.heading: 5.1. Techniques
document_sections.content: The operative approach has changed substantially with technological progress and improved physiological and anatomical understanding. Dandy described anatomical hemispherectomy for a right hemispheric tumor in 1928; McKenzie described its use for epilepsy in 1938, and Krynauw published a pediatric epilepsy cohort in 1950. After decades with few publications, reports from the mid-1990s onward described multiple hemispherectomy and hemispherotomy techniques and their outcomes and complications.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.1. Anatomical hemispherectomy
document_sections.content: The original operation removed a cerebral hemisphere while preserving the basal ganglia. Rasmussen's team subsequently described en bloc removal, as distinct from earlier piecemeal lobar resections. Anatomical hemispherectomy requires extensive exposure, incision and craniotomy from frontal to occipital regions and from near the vertex toward the middle cranial fossa. After dural opening, anterior and middle cerebral arteries are divided and clipped while deep perforators are preserved. Major parasagittal bridging veins are also initially preserved to reduce swelling risk. The surgeon exposes and divides the corpus callosum, enters the frontal horn, disconnects frontobasal tissue, then follows the ventricular anatomy through the trigone and temporal horn toward the anterior hippocampus. Removal commonly proceeds in more than one en bloc stage, isolating the basal ganglia and removing frontal and temporal tissue before parieto-occipital tissue; the insula is generally removed. Classical anatomical hemispherectomy persists in a very small minority of cases, notably for recurrent seizures or HME-associated distortion of anatomy. Despite seizure efficacy, it takes considerable time and carries substantial complications. In 1968, Ignelzi and Bucy proposed hemidecortication, removing only epileptogenic cortex. Adams and colleagues later described reducing the resection cavity by plugging the foramen of Monro and suturing convexity dura to the falx and tentorium; they reported fewer hydrocephalus complications.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.2. Functional hemispherectomy
document_sections.content: Limitations of less extensive anatomical operations led most epilepsy centers from the mid-1990’s to favor functional hemispherectomy or hemispherotomy. Rasmussen first performed a functional operation in 1974, after which multiple variants were described. These approaches rely more on disconnection and less on removal of brain tissue. Along unilateral efferent and commissural structures, they interrupt the corona radiata and internal capsule, frontobasal and temporomesial pathways, insula and corpus callosum. Achieving seizure freedom requires interruption of unilateral projecting pathways, including the cortico-spinal tract, and commissural connections such as the corpus callosum and hippocampal commissure to prevent spread to the opposite hemisphere. Limiting resection is intended particularly to reduce hydrocephalus.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.3. Rasmussen’s functional hemispherectomy (Rasmussen, 1973)
document_sections.content: Rasmussen's procedure combined removal of a broad fronto-dorsal and anterior parietal region with temporal lobectomy, callosotomy and disconnection of remaining frontal, parietal and occipital tissue. Four subsequent functional hemispherotomy approaches are described below.

document_sections.heading: 1. Vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy (Delalande et al., 1992, 2007; Danielpour et al., 2001; Giordano et al., 2015; Baumgartner et al., 2017)
document_sections.content: Delalande and colleagues first described this approach in 1992. With the patient supine and the fixed head slightly flexed, a principally precentral craniotomy permits anterior disconnection; neuronavigation is advisable, especially when anatomy is distorted. A frontal cortical opening averages 5 cm by 3 cm. White-matter dissection enters the lateral ventricle, followed by callosotomy along the ventricular roof through the corpus and splenium, then the genu and rostrum to the anterior commissure. The posterior fornix is divided near the trigone. Disconnection proceeds lateral to the basal ganglia and thalamus along the choroid plexus toward the anterior temporal horn, where the amygdala is resected. Removing posterior gyrus rectus and frontobasal white matter exposes the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and optic nerve; an incision then separates anterior temporal horn fibers from frontobasal cortex. Variants by Danielpour, Giordano and Baumgartner aim to avoid or reduce ventricular entry. For the vertical midline variant, a <10 cm incision above the coronal suture and a 6 cm craniotomy expose the superior sagittal sinus. Interhemispheric exposure precedes callosotomy from rostrum to splenium, using the pericallosal artery and internal cerebral veins/vein of Galen confluence as landmarks. Initial extraventricular dissection near the septum pellucidum limits cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) loss and brain collapse. After opening the ventricle, lateral disconnection follows the choroid plexus from the temporal toward the frontal horn and anterior choroidal point. Anterior disconnection tracks subpially beside the ACA from the cingulum to the frontal base, then laterally toward the carotid bifurcation and back to the anterior commissure; reaching this commissure distinguishes it from the lateral technique. Temporal and fimbria disconnections complete the operation. After hemostasis and saline irrigation, fibrin glue closes ventricular access to help prevent subdural collections.

document_sections.heading: 2. Periinsular hemispherotomy (Villemure and Mascott, 1995; Villemure et al., 2000b)
document_sections.content: The supine patient's head is turned almost horizontally. A Sylvian-centered craniotomy exposes the circular sulcus and frontal and temporal opercula. Resection of these opercula creates two access windows. Through the suprainsular window, removing frontoparietal opercular cortex opens the frontal horn through its anteroposterior extent and interrupts the corona radiata. Intraventricular work then divides the entire corpus callosum, disconnects the splenial fornix-fimbria hippocampi connection and separates anterior frontal tissue toward the sphenoid wing. Through the infrainsular window, superior temporal gyrus (T1) is resected, the temporal horn entered and the uncus, lateral amygdala and anterior hippocampus removed. The insula is aspirated and disconnected at the claustrum/external capsule. A described alternative enters the C-shaped ventricle through a C-shaped corticectomy across F3, supramarginal gyrus and T2. It then disconnects tissue toward the Sylvian fissure from F3 near the foramen Monro and from T2 near the anterior temporal horn, undermines the insula, coagulates and transects the MCA at the insular vallecula, and removes peri-insular tissue and insula en bloc.

document_sections.heading: 3. Transsylvian keyhole functional hemispherectomy (Schramm et al., 1995a, 2001)
document_sections.content: Schramm detailed this variant in 1995 and later reported operative outcomes for 20 cases. A curved frontotemporal incision and small Sylvian- and insular-centered craniotomy make it particularly suitable when the hemisphere is atrophic, as after perinatal ischemia or in RE. Craniotomy dimensions range from 4 × 4 cm to 5 × 6 cm, guided preferably by neuronavigation and by callosal length, mostly 6.5 cm, insular-basal ganglia dimensions and ventricular size. After exposing the Sylvian fissure and circular sulci, the temporal horn is opened through the limen insulae and an unco-amygala-hippocampectomy performed. Opening continues toward the frontal horn, followed by frontobasal disconnection between ACA and MCA landmarks. A complete intraventricular callosotomy proceeds from frontal horn to splenium, initially guided by ACA branches and then the falx. The disconnection follows the falcotentorial junction through the hippocampal tail to the original temporal opening. Major MCA, ACA and posterior cerebral artery (PCA) branches are preserved; insular cortex is aspirated. Frontal operculum may cover the superior circular sulcus by more than 3 cm, compared with 0.5–1.0 cm coverage of the inferior sulcus by temporal operculum. HME is a reason not to use this keyhole approach because enlargement and an atypical insular cistern complicate access. Temporal lobectomy or frontoparietal opercular resection can instead speed surgery and make swelling less problematic. Injury to the healthy opposite hemisphere must be strictly avoided.

document_sections.heading: 4. Japanese modified periinsular hemispherotomy (Shimizu and Maehara, 2000)
document_sections.content: This operation combines features of the peri-insular and Delalande approaches. Its craniotomy covers the anteroposterior extent of the lateral ventricle. Surgeons remove frontal operculum and the upper insular cortex, traverse white matter into the ventricle, perform complete callosotomy and finish with temporomesial disconnection through amygdalo-hippocampectomy. All the described disconnection techniques can be used for HME, but enlargement, possible preoperative midline shift, displacement of the superior sagittal sinus toward the opposite side and indistinct gray-white boundaries complicate surgery. A larger craniotomy and more tissue removal, such as standard temporal lobectomy, are generally recommended. Clipping the MCA or ACA during a larger anatomical resection may reduce bleeding but could increase postoperative ischemia and cerebral edema. Fig. 3 contrasts periinsular with vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy in schematic coronal and axial views.

document_sections.heading: 5.1.4. Postoperative management
document_sections.content: Every patient should spend at least one night in a dedicated medium- or intensive-care unit. Children, especially young infants, may require transfusion. Almost all patients develop a slight temperature rise, attributed to aseptic meningitis from blood products contaminating CSF. One study found that routine external ventricular drainage (EVD) reduced postoperative fever and hydrocephalus. Some centers leave a drain for a couple of days until CSF clears, but clear evidence does not support a recommendation for that practice. Thorough irrigation before closure might help prevent hydrocephalus.

document_sections.heading: 5.2. Techniques – new developments
document_sections.content: Variations of hemispherotomy have appeared during the last 8 years. Kawai and colleagues treated 7 patients using an interhemispheric rather than transcortical route for vertical hemispherotomy and targeted the anterior end of the foramen of Monro rather than the subcallosal region for anterior dissection. They reported less resection and International League Against Epilepsy (ILAE) Class 1 outcomes in 6 out of 7 patients. Giordano and colleagues described an extraventricular route intended especially to lower postoperative hydrocephalus risk. Fig. 4 illustrates coronal and sagittal T1-weighted images after vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.1. Endoscope-assisted hemispherotomy (Wagner et al., 2018)
document_sections.content: Wagner and colleagues reported endoscope-assisted functional hemispherotomy in 2018 for two children with chronic epilepsy after perinatal stroke. Other reports of endoscope-assisted disconnection followed. The main advantage is a smaller incision and craniotomy; the underlying operation resembles vertical parasagittal hemispherotomy. A linear paramedian incision extends 2 cm anterior and 3cm posterior to the coronal suture, with a craniotomy 4 cm long and 2 cm wide. Complete interhemispheric callosotomy precedes ventricular entry, frontobasal disconnection and middle-to-posterior white-matter disconnection between frontal and temporal horns toward the trigone. Amygdala resection and posterior fornix disconnection complete hippocampal disconnection. Longer operating time might increase complications such as infection relative to open surgery, but the limited literature has not clearly established this.

document_sections.heading: 5.2.2. MRgLITT and radiofrequency ablation for functional hemispherotomy (Chua et al., 2020)
document_sections.content: MRI guided laser interstitial thermal therapy (MRgLITT) uses stereotactically placed laser probes and real-time MRI guidance to ablate planned brain regions. Curry and colleagues first reported LITT in 5 children with various lesions in 2012. Subsequent use for periventricular heterotopias, focal cortical dysplasia, tuberous sclerosis and hypothalamic hamartomas has yielded very few studies of longer-term outcomes. A systematic review of laser corpus callosotomy classified all included studies as class IV evidence and called for prospective comparison with open callosotomy. Chua and colleagues described a child with chronic drug-resistant epilepsy whose multiple comorbidities made open disconnection unsuitable. They implanted 5 laser catheters across the hemisphere to disconnect selected areas. As this was a first case, they considered definitive conclusions or advice premature. Chandra subsequently used robotic radiofrequency (RF) thermocoagulation according to a similar technical concept.

document_sections.heading: 6. Complications: an overview and a consensus on their avoidance
document_sections.content: Knowledge of complications informs candidate selection, early recognition, management and prevention. Anatomical hemispherectomy has been associated with mortality reported at 2 to 10 % in earlier publications, attributed in part to extensive removal, sagittal sinus injury and major bleeding, and sacrifice of cortical veins followed by severe edema. Later hemispherotomy series report much lower mortality: Schramm and colleagues found 1.0 % in a large retrospective pediatric series and 0 % in an adult series at the same center; other recent pediatric series reported 0 %. Less extensive resection, avoidance of coagulating cortical vessels of the affected hemisphere and advances in neuroanesthesia may help explain the decrease. Reported morbidity spans surgical, neurological, neuro-endocrinological and neurocognitive events. Especially after anatomical hemispherectomy, complications include superficial cerebral hemosiderosis, major bleeding and transfusion, shunt-requiring hydrocephalus, hematoma, persistent fever and infection. Some authors question whether superficial cerebral hemosiderosis was present in historical series; recent pediatric and adult series report no cases, perhaps because tissue injury and blood loss were reduced. Hypothalamic injury during frontal disconnection can cause SIADH or DI, severe hypo- or hypernatremia and even sinus thrombosis. Major blood loss can also produce tachycardia, circulatory instability, metabolic acidosis, hypothermia and serious electrolyte disturbance. Brian and colleagues reported transfusions in every patient in an older series; Gowda and colleagues likewise reported transfusions in all their patients, who were under 6 months old. Roth and colleagues reported transfusion in all children operated on before 3 months. Blood loss and transfusion needs have decreased with less resective operations, particularly lateral keyhole and vertical approaches, possibly because exposure and incisions are smaller. Lee and colleagues reported hydrocephalus in 9–81 % of mixed adult and pediatric populations and 23 % of pediatric patients. Brotis and colleagues reported 2–26 %; later pediatric series reported around 13–14 %, while a review by Lopez and colleagues found 19 % overall. HME and multifocal cortical dysplasia have been proposed as risk factors for hydrocephalus and shunt placement. Evidence about EVD conflicts: one report found no apparent reduction in definitive postoperative hydrocephalus, whereas another center reported a reduction. Postoperative hematoma, infection and fever contribute to cumulative surgical morbidity after either operation. Schramm and colleagues reported 7.4 % in adults and 9.7 % in children; Ye and colleagues reported 10 % for hematoma/hygroma/infection, and Weil and colleagues reported 14.8 % in children. A series restricted to reoperations reported 28.5 % surgical complications. Across 37 pediatric series, Lopez and colleagues found hematoma rates of 10 to 36 %, infection rates of 2 % to 7 %, and persistent fever in up to 83 %. They associated HME and SWS more frequently with hematoma and RE with fever. Kamath and colleagues also reported more fever with RE, less severe fever with cortical dysplasia or polymicrogyria, and possible fever reduction with EVD. Younger age has been proposed as another surgical complication risk. Permanent worsening or new hemiparesis has been reported in 8–21 %: pediatric reports found 8 % and 10 %, while an adult series reported 21 %. Patients remained able to walk even when pre-existing weakness worsened. An adult series reported postoperative speech or language worsening in 10 %, as well as temporary spontaneously resolving mutism; language problems were more frequent after dominant-side surgery. Pediatric visual studies reported new or worsened strabismus in 49 %, with compensatory torticollis in the vast majority of those affected, and decreased visual acuity in 56 % with new visual field deficits in 71 % in another series. Complete hemispheric disconnection inevitably causes postoperative hemianopia, although function is often preserved through compensation and strabismus correction may not be needed. Contralateral motor loss and language deterioration are harder to predict before surgery; younger children may ultimately improve linguistically beyond their preoperative level. Neurocognitive effects have not been adequately studied, and lack of reports does not establish lack of effect. Comparisons among techniques are confounded by differences in patients, underlying disease, seizure-onset age, anti-seizure medication (ASM) and operations. Limbrick and colleagues found no difference in pediatric complication incidence by technique; Kwan and colleagues reported fewer complications with peri-insular surgery, whereas Iwasaki and colleagues found fewer perioperative complications with vertical hemispherotomy. Small, retrospective and heterogeneous series do not support statistically strong conclusions. Finally, coagulation of perforators near the anterior communicating artery complex or ACA during frontobasal disconnection can cause hypothalamic ischemia, SIADH, cerebral salt wasting or diabetes insipidus. Resulting severe hypo- or hypernatremia and refractory edema can progress to coma and death.

document_sections.heading: 7. Current practice in Europe
document_sections.content: A survey containing 12 questions was circulated among geographically dispersed European epilepsy surgery centers; Table 1 provides center-level responses. In most participating countries epilepsy surgery is centralized, and one surgeon performs these operations at most centers (N = 20/27, 74 %). Most centers began between 1980 and 2000 (N = 16/27 centers; 59 %); eight centers (37 %) began between 2000 and 2010, and three centers (11 %) after 2010. The main approaches are lateral transsylvian and vertical parasagittal disconnection with variants, and choice depends strongly on where surgeons trained. Only lateral transsylvian surgery was used in 13 centers (n = 13/27; 48 %), only vertical parasagittal surgery in eight (n = 8/27; 30 %), and both in six (22 %). Thirteen centers (48 %) operated only on children, thirteen (48 %) on children and adults, and one (4 %) only on adults. Almost all centers (96 %) treated classical causes of catastrophic drug-resistant epilepsy arising from one hemisphere. Over the last 5–10 years, 15 centers (56 %) reported increased volume, nine (33 %) no change and three (11 %) a decrease. Hemispheric surgery is exceptionally complex and requires an experienced interdisciplinary team and specialized intraoperative and postoperative facilities. Surgeons should complete extensive training with an experienced colleague before undertaking it; collaboration with other specialized centers is common. Long-term seizure outcomes for minimally invasive approaches remain unknown because reports consist of cases or small series; collaboration among high-volume centers may clarify them.

document_sections.heading: 8. Strengths and limitations
document_sections.content: The statement combines an international European collaboration, peer-reviewed literature, authors' accumulated clinical experience and accounts from established European epilepsy centers under the EANS functional neurosurgery section. The literature is extensive but heterogeneous and was used to support the discussion. Because the conditions requiring hemispheric disconnection are rare and complex, obtaining high-level evidence is difficult. The center questionnaire was intended to describe present practice and inform the topics reviewed.

document_sections.heading: 9. Conclusion
document_sections.content: The authors present this as the first European consensus addressing the history, indications, techniques and complications of hemispheric disconnection for chronic drug-resistant epilepsy from different causes, alongside an overview of practice at established European centers. They conclude that long-term postoperative seizure outcomes can currently be established only for open disconnection and its technical variants. Minimally invasive approaches are developing rapidly, but published experience comprises individual cases or small series and does not yet establish long-term seizure outcomes.
